scenes.heading: select Statement
scenes.narration: Let's explore the select statement, the control structure that lets a goroutine wait on several channel operations at once.

scenes.heading: What select does
items: Waits on multiple channel operations at once
Proceeds with whichever is ready first
If several are ready, picks one at random
scenes.narration: A plain receive can only wait on one channel. Select solves that: it blocks until one of its case operations can proceed, then runs exactly that case. If several are ready at the same moment it chooses one uniformly at random, which prevents starvation. And adding a default case makes select non-blocking — default runs immediately when nothing else is ready.

scenes.heading: How select chooses a case
steps: Register the goroutine on each wait queue
Park until some channel is ready
If several ready, shuffle and pick one
Complete that case, leave the others
scenes.narration: Internally the runtime evaluates every case's channel expression once, registers the goroutine on each channel's wait queue, and parks it. When any channel becomes ready it wakes the goroutine, completes that one operation, and removes it from the other queues. If multiple are ready at registration time, it shuffles the case order and picks the first — that is where the randomness comes from.

scenes.heading: Bounding work with a timeout
scenes.narration: This is the canonical timeout pattern. We race the work channel against time.After, which returns a channel that fires once after the duration. Because the worker sleeps fifty milliseconds but the timeout is only ten, the timeout case wins and we print timed out. Racing work against a timer is how you protect against slow dependencies without blocking forever.

scenes.text: select does NOT try cases top-to-bottom — among ready cases it picks at random. And empty select{} blocks forever.
scenes.narration: Two things trip people up. Select does not evaluate cases in top-to-bottom order; among ready cases it picks at random, so you cannot rely on case order for priority. And an empty select with no cases does not do nothing — it blocks forever, deadlocking the goroutine.

scenes.text: Wrap select in a for loop with a ctx.Done() case — the standard leak-free event loop.
scenes.narration: The workhorse pattern is a for-select loop: each iteration handles whichever channel is ready, including a case on ctx.Done that returns to stop cleanly. That gives long-lived goroutines a responsive, leak-free exit path.
